newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Fischler revives old ideas to face farming future.
newsitem.headline: Fischler revives old ideas to face farming future.

text.p: As the European Commission prepares reluctant farmers to meet major new challenges at the start of the 21st century, it is resurrecting old ideas such as targetting aid on those who need it most.

EU farmers will have to face increasing competition as the World Trade Organisation prises open agricultural markets, the EU expands eastwards to take in up to 10 former communist countries and budgetary constraints tighten.
Targetting aid -- so-called modulation -- on the smallest and poorest farmers, was one of the key ideas of the 1992 farm reform package.

But the idea was buried after Britain and France, which have a relatively high proportion of large farms, complained about discrimination, saying it would sharply cut set-aside and other aid payments to their cereals farmers.
"Modulation... was sacrificed on the altar of the 'level playing field,'" EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said this week.
Speaking in Prague, Fischler said there was growing criticism in the press and rural communities about some wealthy landowners receiving huge set-aside handouts.
"This does not help create a positive image for farming in the EU and can make enemies at a time when friends are needed to improve the system," he told a conference.
"In this area too, I will give careful consideration to all the arguments for and against," he said.
The rejection of modulation by EU farm ministers meant that the 20 percent wealthiest and most productive farmers continued to claim 80 percent of farm set-aside subsidies.
But the ministers did agree to a major change in support -- introducing area-based, instead of production-linked, payments to compensate for a 34 percent reduction in intervention prices.
The Commission believes that compensation payments target farmers more efficiently and reduce the scope for fraud as they are not linked to export subsidies.
"Fields and animals are easier to control than sealed containers crossing frontiers or bulk cargoes sailing around the world," Fischler said.

But continued compensation for price cuts agreed in 1992 are becoming increasingly difficult to defend against criticism from taxpayers and consumers, especially after world cereals prices soared to record levels earlier this year.
Fischler suggested that direct payments to farmers could continue to be justified as recompense for their role in looking after the countryside and keeping rural areas alive.

"Farmers occupy the land and should continue to do so if we want to keep the kind of countryside we have created over the centuries in Europe and not allow our rural lanscape to revert to wilderness," he said.
Direct payments to farmers would also help to ease the transition from highly subsidised to market-oriented farming.
"They provide the security that allows businesses and not bankruptcies to flourish," Fischler said.
But for the immediate, the priority is to introduce reforms to curb beef surpluses and restore consumer confidence undermined by the mad cow public health scare.
